Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, August 13, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke to the country about actions which the government was taking as a result of a comprehensive review of its expenditure and revenue patterns.
He pointed out that the review had disclosed, in particular, three compelling facts. First, almost without exception, this decade has been characterized by yearly budgetary deficits exceeding $4 billion in total and requiring upwards of $400 million per annum to service.
Second, despite a buoyant economy, increases in taxation and rapidly growing revenues, expenditures have shown a continuing tendency to outstrip revenues. Analysis shows that this phenomenon has resulted mainly from a rapid and larger than anticipated growth in certain large programs which the federal government shares with the provinces. Expenditures for such programs as hospital insurance, the Canada Assistance Plan, post-secondary education, and now Medicare, are projected to grow at a much more rapid rate than the increase in revenues at current tax rates. This means that unless taxes are to be increased further or savings are found elsewhere, the country will be faced with the situation of chronic and growing deficits in our public accounts.
Third, while new programs and activities are being introduced, old programs continue to grow with very little evidence that these were subjected to careful evaluation and scrutiny to see whether they are as relevant

October 31, 1969
The Address-Mr. Drury today as when they were introduced, or whether they have now served their purpose and should be eliminated or curtailed.
No government and no institution can afford to do at once all of the worth-while things that it would like to do and which it is requested to do. This means that governments must plan to ensure that, within the means available, those things are accomplished that are most urgent and most desirable.
Governments must ensure that their scarce resources are being applied to the most urgent and useful purposes. In light of this background, the government concluded that deficits could not be allowed to continue year in and year out and that, in current economic circumstances, the appropriate manner to remove the prospect of a deficit was by controlling assiduously the expenditure side of the budget.
Some high priority programs, including the shared-cost programs which I have mentioned, will require increased expenditure. But the majority of programs and activities cannot be allowed to increase in expenditure if we are to reach our budgetary objectives without an increase in taxation. The government, therefore, has set as its main guideline for preparation of the 1970-71 estimates the requirement that all programs and activities not referred to for specific treatment in other guidelines, would be frozen at current levels of expenditure.
What does this mean in clear, simple terms? This means that all cost increases, including salary increases, must be absorbed within the limits imposed by the dollar levels reflected in the 1969-70 estimates. This will necessitate painful reductions in operating budgets; the items for travel, advertising, use of consultants, supplies of all kinds and so forth. Far more important, it means a reduction in the size of the public service. Because salaries constitute the largest single item in operating budgets, departments will have to cut their work force in order to live within these dollar limits.
There has been a great deal of speculation about what this will mean, and prophets of gloom and doom have been raising the spectre of thousands of public servants being summarily dismissed from their jobs by a callous and unfeeling government. What are the facts?
Before the beginning of this fiscal year, the government reduced authorized levels in the public service by about 9,000 man-years. The government has since decided that, of the
IMr. Drury.]
positions that were vacant at the end of July, more than 10,000 will not be filled. For the coming year, the expenditure ceilings resulting from our hold-the-line guideline will mean, as the Prime Minister stated, from
5.000	to 7,000 fewer people on the federal payroll than there were at the end of July. Taken together, these reductions add up to
25.000	jobs, or a 10 per cent decrease from the 1968 authorized size of the public service.
I hasten to emphasize that this does not mean that 25,000 employees will lose their jobs. Nor does it mean that even 5,000 will be laid off. Normal attrition through retirement, resignations and the like amount to about 10 per cent of the work force each year. This has greatly facilitated the adjustments required in the past year and will facilitate those that will have to take place in the coming months. There will be some lay-offs. This is so because the jobs which become vacant through attrition are not necessarily in those programs where reductions will have to be made and the skills required to fill these positions may not be those possessed, even with retraining, by employees in other programs affected by the guideline.
To give an example, if a doctor leaves the public service and is to be replaced, it would be impossible to fill his position by transferring an employee from a program in which there were some cut-backs unless that employee is a doctor. This task of matching surplus employees with vacancies occurring through attrition is one which the Treasury Board, the departments and the Public Service Commission are dealing with, and the completion of which is fundamental to determining how many employees and of what kind will be able to be re-assigned or relocated.
This process is now going forward and the number can only be determined as departments complete adjusting their programs to these guidelines. I might emphasize here that, while the numbers game captures headlines and provides a certain dramatic interest, our main concern is with the individual.
Given the fact that the expenditure guidelines would necessitate a reduction in the size and composition of the public service, and knowing that the effects of the guidelines would vary among departments and among occupational groups, the government announced its decision immediately it was taken in order that departments would have the maximum amount of time to plan adjustments in their programs; that individual

employees would be made aware at the earliest possible date; and so that consultations with employee organizations could begin as soon as possible.
Within a few days after the government announcement in August, consultations began with employee organizations to discuss and develop personnel policies that the government should adopt with a view to, firstly, enabling departments and agencies to adjust their use of manpower to the new financial limits and government objectives and, secondly, to deal fairly with the employees directly affected and keep to a minimum the disruption of their employment in the public service.
These consultations took place over a period of several weeks. Many useful proposals were made by the employee organizations and were incorporated into the policies and procedures which are being applied to the handling of manpower adjustments. While it is perhaps to be expected that the employee organizations would have preferred a policy of no lay-offs, I think that it is correct to say that, in the circumstances, they would agree that the policies and procedures adopted go a long way toward dealing fairly and equitably with the employees affected.

Surplus employees are being given first consideration for re-assignment to jobs for which they are qualified as positions become vacant in their own or other departments. The Treasury Board has requested the Public Service Commission to take action to restrict or suspend hirings and promotions in affected occupational groups and levels, as required, to facilitate the re-assignment of surplus employees.
Departments having requirements for new employees must seek them first from among the surplus employees reported to the commission. Re-assignment will be made not only within a department or between departments in a particular location but, if need be,
The Address-Mr. Drury between departments at different locations, although re-assignments will be attempted in such a way as to keep to a minimum changes in employees' jobs, occupations, departments and locations. Relocation expenses will be paid to employees who have to move and departments have been advised how to deal with these situations in detail. I might mention that these arrangements were also arrived at following consultations with employee organizations.
Departments have been directed to identify surplus employees as soon as possible so that there will be maximum time to attempt re-assignment and give maximum notification to the employees affected. Employees will be given at least three months' notice that they are surplus to requirements, and in many cases it will be possible to give longer periods of notice. During this period, every effort will be made to find other jobs for the employees affected.
Departments are keeping employees informed of the progress being made in attempting their re-assignment. If re-assignment is not possible, any lay-offs which take place will be according to the merit principles which govern order of lay-offs and which are set out in the Public Service Employment regulations.
It has been alleged that the government was firing all employees age 60 and over. Nothing could be further from the truth. It did seem, however, to make sense for departments to review the situation in respect of employees in this group, having in mind that there could be less hardship occasioned by the retirement of such an employee than by the lay-off of another employee whose length of service or other circumstances might be less favourable. Departments have been advised to take all factors into account, as well as departmental operational requirements.
It should be clear from what I have said that we cannot yet determine in any precise way how many employees may be separated from the public service. Certainly, it is my sincere hope and expectation that the measures adopted will keep the number to a minimum. Nevertheless, I think we must proceed in the manner that we have begun, because not to do so would be to avoid our responsibility to the public at large for greater efficiency in government departments and agencies and higher productivity from each person on the government payroll.

I hope I made it clear that a softening of attitude was not needed. The hon. member is aware, I think, that under the superannuation legislation public servants earn the right to a pension payable at the age of 60 or after. Those who are separated from the public service at 60 or over qualify for, and will receive, an immediate pension. Those who are separated from the public service earlier-and I myself am in that category- qualify for a pension payable only when they reach the age of 60. This means that a man separated before he reaches the age of 60 does not qualify for an immediate pension. Obviously, he would suffer greater hardship than the man who gets an immediate pension on separation.
The age 60 group was mentioned in the light of the fact that the immediate pension is payable in respect of these people whereas those who have not reached that age have the right to a deferred pension payable at the age of 60.

25,000	employees a year. In fact, some 25,000 people leave the public service each year because of death, retirement, resignation or dismissal. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I would like to associate myself with the congratulations that have been extended to the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Mar-ceau) on their splendid addresses at the opening of this debate. I think there was a comment in Time magazine, just after the last election, to the effect that there was nothing that the Canadian people like to do more than to elect a conservative in the guise of a reformer. It is in the light of those remarks that I should like to review some of our progress to date, some of the anticipated progress we are going to make as outlined in the Speech from the Throne, and perhaps I should also say something about our lack of progress.
To begin, let me say that I think that remark in the magazine, to a large extent is wrong. We have been a reform government and have passed, and we anticipate passing,
October 31, 1969

progressive legislation. Some of it will probably be the most progressive legislation that this nation has ever seen. We have changed some of the rules of this institution. Putting the emphasis on committee work has given far greater scope to individual members of parliament than they had before to do a more effective job.
We have also changed some aspects of the criminal law which were long overdue for change. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) are to be congratulated on the omnibus bill they presented to the house during the last session.
Some of the decisions that have been made have taken courage. The decision to exchange ambassadors with the Vatican took courage, though I personally do not agree with what was done. The introduction of the bilingualism bill took courage and shows that the government is capable of exercising courage when required to do so.
We have also moved toward a more suitable constitution for the country, another change long overdue. We all look forward to a new constitution within our time. We have a new, progressive Indian policy which will lift these people up and fit them into society to take the rightful position they so much deserve. We are also doing something about regional development. I note from the Speech from the Throne that the government is considering future policy in depth and hopes to meet the coming challenge of the post-industrial era.
After a little dynamite and shotgunning from the back benches, the government has made a declaration of Arctic sovereignty, probably the first nationalistic step that this country has taken in a number of years. So, taken all in all, I think that we have made good progress.
But if I were to give my speech a theme, I should like to say that I do not think we have moved either fast or far enough, and that I am not so sure that we are always moving in the right direction. We know we are living in a rapidly changing society, one that is changing in many ways. The hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens), in his splendid address last night, showed the house how we are changing to an urbanized society from a rural one.
We are also changing in our private lives. We are changing from the static authoritarianism of the past to the humanism of today. No longer will people permit their lives to be controlled by dogmatic and institutionally

The Address-Mr. Hogarth imposed ethical and moral concepts. The ethical and moral evaluations of modern western man are more and more becoming matters of individual choice, rather than the submissive acceptance of the dictates of religion and government.
Although there are good aspects about this change, there are also bad aspects. Where the good aspects lie are in the fact that man is freer to seek the free expression of his unique personality, the process that psychologists tell us is one of self-realization. The bad aspects result in permissiveness, escapism, alienation from purpose, lack of social responsibility, and refusal to sacrifice for the common good. These evils result in disrespect for authority and for the institutions it represents, of which parliament is one. People are impatient for change.
One bad aspect of humanism is that in many instances people have contempt for law and order and show violence in their expression of dissent. Another bad aspect of humanism is the nihilism and escapism which is symptomized by the common use of drugs in our society today. There is an undue emphasis on pornography and obscenity in the arts and cultural media. It seems that this results in a world in which everybody is out for themselves, and this reflects itself in many of our labour disputes where there is complete contempt for responsibility and the innocent victims of mass strikes.
Politicians at all levels of government must be aware of this changing scene. They must be aware of its good and of its evils. The real challenge that is facing us today as responsible politicians is to be able to recognize the nature of this changing world, to be able to see its true meaning and its essence. In drafting our laws and our legislative programs we must suit the society for which they are designed and provide good government.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that this takes a certain amount of political genius. A reformer in a static society has a relatively easy job to do. But in the volatile boiling pot of the western world, and particularly Canada which is cursed with historical factionalism, with geographic, ethnic and religious differences and with a residual of authoritarianism, it is a very tough job.
There are one or two aspects of the Speech from the Throne that would lead me to believe that perhaps we have not seen this challenge to which I refer in its proper light. Mention is made of the unrest among our young people, with which we are all concerned. This is a symptom of the transition of
October 31, 1969

The Address-Mr. Hogarth which I have spoken. At page 2 of Hansard for October 23 appears this paragraph:
A disturbing element in many countries of the world has been the rising tide of unrest, particularly among young people. It has expressed itself in many ways, in public debate, in peaceful protest and sometimes in violence. Our profound disapproval of the excesses must not blind us to deeply felt and legitimate aspirations. Many citizens in our own country believe that they are entitled to assume greater responsibility for the destiny of our society. Such demands, in so far as they do not conflict with the general welfare, are the expression of a truly democratic ideal. They must be satisfied if our society is to attain its goals of peace and justice.
This is exactly what the activists have been saying. The expression "such demands, in so far as they do not conflict with the general welfare" indicates to me that the government is going to remain the final arbiter of what general welfare is. It is the "establishment" that determines what is general welfare. It appears to me that the inference there is that, unless the young people stay within the framework of those concepts that we have decided shall govern in the future, then reforms and activism are unacceptable.
I do not think this is the way we should look at reform. Neither do I think it is the way we should look at our changing society. After all, what have we done for our young people? Following those euphemistic words in the Speech from the Throne the only provision we made for them was the lowering of the voting age to 18. We must go much further than this, and not only in parliament; we must go further in our political processes. We must encourage our young people to join political parties. Although everyone says we do this, we must make sure we provide the structure that will allow them to voice their requirements. Through their vote they can influence government.
A young person who joins a political party today has a difficult time in getting his views adopted. If he is successful in getting a resolution passed, it is not binding on the government of the day, even if it is his own party that is in power. Modest steps have been taken in our caucus to correct this situation. We are looking forward to reforms that will at last permit elected representatives to have a say in government policy. But that is not enough. We should have our political processes structured from the grass roots to the East Block so these things are acceptable and understood.

[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Another passage from the speech is most disconcerting. We have put some emphasis on reforms to the Criminal Law and these are long overdue. The speech outlines what we mean by this in the following sentences:
The size, complexity and fallability of the structures that technology imposes on modern societies are often in conflict with the protection and development of individual values. The workings of both private and public institutions may endanger the individual's free expression of his unique personality. He must therefore be protected from anything that jeopardizes his rights or limits his personal development.
What do we do? It appears that the elephant has given birth to a rabbit. The only reforms we have are amendments to the Criminal Code pertaining to bail and wire tapping. We have an also ran from the Solicitor General's department dealing with pardons, which is really only going to have a psychological effect. We have also a bill from the Senate on hate literature. When you consider what is necessary, you must realize that these reforms are pitifully inadequate. Oddly enough, we use the most altruistic motives but you will note that not one of these amendments is going to cost any money. If we are going to have Criminal Law reform and justice, we must be prepared to meet the cost.
Consider what we should be doing. In 1929 the Juvenile Delinquents Act was passed. It was known early in the game that it was not satisfactory, and it certainly is not satisfactory now. In 1965, four years ago, we had a departmental committee set up which prepared an excellent report after travelling all over Canada discussing these problems with sociologists, lawyers and judges. That report was filed in 1965 but nothing has been done since 1965 about that Act. We should have it before us this session, and it should have been before Parliament at the last one. We wonder what the delay is and why it is not before us.
Let us consider the Ouimet report which we received ten days ago. I was pleased to hear the Solicitor General (Mr. Mellraith) say today, and I note he is in the house, that he is open for suggestions as to what to do with it. That very splendid report should have been automatically referred to a standing committee of this house, or we should have a special committee set up to consider it. The reforms in it are far-reaching and if we do not get at it soon, by the time we do get at it the reforms it suggests will themselves need reforming.
October 31, 1969

We need a national criminal legal aid scheme. Provincial legal aid should be subsidized and integrated with a national scheme like medicare. It is disgraceful to see accused persons try to defend themselves on serious charges. This is our responsibility. We give the accused the right to a full answer in defence by counsel learned in the law. The accused then asks where his counsel is, and finds he does not have one. We will provide the judge, we will provide the police witnesses and even in federal cases we provide the prosecutors, but we do not provide counsel for the accused.
At the justice committee last year we disciplined ourselves to considering solely what was in the Omnibus Bill. Time and time again it was pointed out to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) that other sections of the Criminal Code should be amended. The wording of the Criminal Code is disgraceful. We were told these amendments would be made during the next session and that there would be a mini-bill. It is not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. I think it should be before this house now because these things were drawn to the attention of the Department of Justice and agreed upon in some instances.
We need reform of our laws dealing with the criminally insane. We treat them like pigs. We incarcerate them in isolation and wish that somehow this whole matter would go away because it is not a human problem. We need reform. We need extensive research into psychopathic criminal behaviour, we need research in respect of psychopathic sexual behaviour. What is causing it and what can be done to prevent it? We must find out how we can avoid the terrors of this particular type of criminal activity.
I am surprised that after the rape of Montreal we are not giving some attention to a change in our laws pertaining to riots and disorders. These laws are somewhat archaic if you take a good look at them. I am surprised that we have not got an extension to Section 70 of the Criminal Code so that policemen who have a responsibility must obey that responsibility or get out of the police force. I am surprised that we have not extended that section so we might prevent riots and civil disorders. Our judges are not properly paid. This government is niggardly in respect of judges. They are not being properly paid in comparison with the earnings of men of similar experience in the legal profession.
We should abolish corporal punishment. Why do we not meet these challenges? Why

The Address-Mr. Hogarth do we not at least put them up for debate? In any event, we need abolition of corporal punishment. There have been bills before parliament for years providing for the abolition of this prehistoric device which never works at the best of times. These are just a few of the fields we should be dealing with in the area of Criminal Law. Like the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) wished to do, I could go on all day.
I am proud of what the Speech from the Throne says, but I am somewhat ashamed by what it does not say and what it should be saying. If we would be reformers we have to give some attention to what is holding things up and what is the missing cog in the machine. I think one hang-up is our failure to examine closely the mechanics by which this institution operates, by which change could rapidly take place and by which there could be action and reaction to public demands within a reasonable period of time instead of years. I think we are constipated by tradition and fear of action; tradition that is meaningless in modern Canada and fear of action which shows a lack of feeling of national destiny.
Some of the rules of this house are quaint. Rule 28 says that any member wishing to speak shall rise uncovered. We stopped wearing hats in the House of Commons years ago. That is just a trivial example of many of the archaic things in those rules. Some of the trappings of the house look as though they came out of the pages of Treasure Island.
We should never have abolished the committee we set up during the last session to consider changes in the rules of this house. It should be a standing committee so that these rules might be constantly under review. It probably could give attention to some of the problems of the house.
One of the greatest obstructions to change in Canada today is the fantastic bureaucracy of the Canadian Civil Service. The Canadian Civil Service taken as a whole, with some notable exceptions, has not had an original idea since Confederation, and that came from an Englishman. The odd thing is that these public servants never get fired. The rarest thing in the Canadian Civil Service is a rolling head. This just does not happen. These Civil servants are either promoted, put somewhere else or drafted into some research station where nobody ever sees them again, but they are still paid. Some of them show true genius-true genius at making excuses and causing delay. We have all had experience with these people at committee meetings
October 31. 1969

The Address-Mr. Hogarth when considering a minister's estimates. A civil servant, knowing he is going to get into a little hot water and knowing also that a member has only 10 minutes to ask questions, is very good at taking 10 minutes to give his first two names. You never do really find out who he is.
The real fear, however, and the real blame rests to a great extent on ourselves. We have to take a great deal of the blame. We also are afraid to abandon the baby blankets of the past. We are afraid to attack conventional wisdom. We are afraid of what political effect this is going to have in our ridings. That is what we are afraid of. We are afraid to stand up and make statements that we know might not be acceptable, even though we know they are morally and logically sound. We are terribly afraid of political introspection. We have too much pragmatism and compromise, and not enough principle. Compromise is a political device, not a principle at all. This brings about half-baked programs.
Look at what we did finally with the languages bill last year when we compromised. Section 11(1), as a result of a compromise made by this government with the western At' orneys-General, ended up by providing that in a bilingual district an accused person or a witness, has the right to speak either of these two important languages. However, when the accused is addressing the court or a jury, he has no such right. This is left to the discretion of the court. That was the result of the compromise. You can see what compromise can do to principle.
[DOT] (f2:50 p.m.)
We act out of sentimentality fostered by public opinion that can be swayed and distorted by false and fraudulent facts promulgated by the mass media. A prize example of this sort of action was the cancellation of the seal hunt. It was so sentimental I am surprised it was not announced by Mickey Mouse or Smokey the Bear, because those of us who went into that problem in depth found there was no cruelty to animals. We found conservation was being practised and we found it was an economic thing for the people to be doing. I wonder if we will cancel all the trapping and killing of animals in Canada. If we were to follow that principle we would be in serious trouble in respect of many of the industries.
We are too parochial. We fail to see this country as a country which in the existential sense is in the process of "becoming". We lack healthy nationalism. Those of us on the back bench who advocated the proclamation

of Arctic sovereignty last spring were, as reported in the press, referred to as ultra-nationalists. I am proud to be an ultra-nationalist if this results in the announcements that have been made recently on this subject.
Canadians have dealt for years somewhat harshly with their would-be activists and would-be reformers. We have always been very cautious of them. I was wondering the other day what Louis Riel, one of the great Canadian activists, would think if he were here now. He would say, "Today the scaffold, tomorrow the monument, the day after tomorrow the postage stamp".

speechtext:
Thank you for recognizing me, Mr. Speaker. I join my colleagues in congratulating the hon. members for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) for their contributions which set the high tone of this debate. I must also express my appreciation to other hon. members who have spoken thus far. They have spoken sincerely and their speeches have been of high calibre. I congratulate those who have been appointed Parliamentary Secretaries. I wish them luck. I wish the two Ministers without Portfolio from urban ridings in Toronto and Windsor well. I earnestly hope they do not become frustrated
October 31, 1969

The Address-Mr. Alexander because of this government's evident lack of interest in urban progress. I will not repeat what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and others have said so eloquently about the Speech from the Throne, that it is full of pious platitudes. I agree with that. It contains good points, however, one of them being that the government has at last recognized the young people of this country and will give them the opportunity of taking advantage of the franchise. Let it be known, Mr. Speaker, that at the Niagara Conference of October 9, 10 and 11, this party laid down the guidelines on this question. This government has not suddently thought of this matter. It has been thought of before.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was thought of in Saskatchewan 20 years ago.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I share in the concern of young people who say that they should have the opportunity to run their own affairs. They want to participate in the directing of this country's affairs and to play a significant role. We are privileged and honoured, because in this country we have young people with special talents. I say this with all sincerity, because it was as a result of the vim and vitality of the young people in my constituency that I was elected to the House of Commons. For that I am extremely grateful. Our young people will not remain patient in the face of injustice and will not settle for token measures that only gloss over and do not solve problems. Many of them are disillusioned with "the establishment". I say to them, "You will be part of the establishment once you have the franchise." If they are disappointed with the performance of any elected member, they should kick him out. That is ah there is to it. If they do not know how to go about that, they should speak to the seasoned politician-and I consider myself a seasoned politician since I have finished my one year apprenticeship stint in this House. We will show our young people whom they should back and whom they should not back. They should not vote for those who are incapable of giving proper direction to the affairs of this country.
The Speech from the Throne referred to pollution, a matter of high priority. Having read several articles on the subject and having seen several documentaries in the last two or three years, I have concluded that if we do not begin solving the problem of pollution in the next three or four years we may have nothing at all, literally, to worry about in 25 years time. We must show concern not

only in respect of water pollution but various forms of pollution that affect the earth, the air and our environment. We have all heard about noise, visual pollution and even mental pollution. We know the problems. To discover them we do not need to conduct a great deal of research or intensive study. I think it would be well if this government were to create a separate ministry responsible for pollution, to co-ordinate and bring under one authority the anti-pollution programs of other departments of government. That way the federal government could set standards. Penalties for infractions of the regulations could also be established. We must keep in mind that provincial governments will have set up their own antipollution programs and that local authorities concerned with pollution have introduced specific anti-pollution measures. You know, Mr. Speaker, about 200 agencies are concerned with pollution. Surely, the federal government could step into the picture, give leadership, and co-ordinate the activities of the various bodies in this nation in the fight against pollution. That way we could correlate all the information about pollution that has been gathered, and pass this information on to those interested in the matter.
Although this government may express interest in the subject of pollution, I doubt its sincerity in solving the problem. On the one hand, we have the centre devoted to the study of inland waters at Burlington, where the government will spend millions of dollars on research into pollution; and, on the other hand, we have the case of the City of Hamilton. The city knew what its problem was and decided to call tenders in the early part of 1970 for the completion of a secondary sewage plant, but this government said, "No". I remember asking the Minister without Portfolio responsible for housing about this matter, and in a pious-sounding answer he as much as said, "There is no sense in undertaking this project now." I ask, what is of prime importance in our fight against pollution?

Another area that has been dealt with in the Throne Speech is housing. This government has indicated its desire to see one million housing units built within the next five years. This is commendable, but we have been telling this government all along that there has been a housing crisis. This is an area which we should move into quickly, and I will have more to say about that later.
There are other objectives mentioned in the Throne Speech which are admirable such as
October 31, 1969

those with respect to tax reform and the war against inflation. Whether we are proceeding in the right way remains to be seen. What strikes me as being extremely significant is the fact that Anthony Westall, a man whose ability I can appreciate, sums up the speech in this way:
"The Trudeau government remains today without a clear image-Is it progressive or reactionary?- and without a social message for Canadians".
The latter part is extremely important, "without a social message for Canadians". As I understand it, Mr. Speaker, this government is going through a planning stage. This government spent its first year in power clearing up old business, finding the problems and then attempting to slit the throat of the opposition by the imposition of 75c. speechtext:
The second year, Mr. Speaker, will be taken up with the discussion of solutions; the third year with putting through legislation, and the fourth year with sitting back and gloating over their marvellous contribution. Then, the government will go to the people.
I cannot say anything against planning, Mr. Speaker. Planning is always required. However, there are certain areas in which we must move away from too rigid a stand. There are many areas which this government will now have to take into consideration. They will have to forget they are at the planning stage because they are also at the problem, solution and legislation stages today.
Action is needed, Mr. Speaker, particularly in two areas, unemployment and the complexities of urban growth. This is the great tragedy of that Speech from the Throne. For some reason or other, there was a lack of recognition of these two very important crises in the Canadian economy. If this government promised anything, Mr. Speaker, it promised to govern and create. They were going to create a new Canadian society, but how can you create a new Canadian society without the recognition of the great sprawling urban problems?
A society, just or otherwise, can only develop on a foundation of healthy economic growth and that means job opportunity, decent annual incomes, steady demand, steady production and last, but not least, equality of opportunity to share in national development and prosperity. No society can
The Address-Mr. Alexander be termed just that contains within it the regional disparities that we find in Canada. No society can be truly just that can callously write off, for the sake of convenience, primary industries that happen to have fallen on evil days and whole sections of the population who, through no fault of their own, happen to share this state.
From reading the representations of the Economic Council over the years it is seen that the term "full employment" is continually emphasized. This phrase is coupled with a strong affirmation that it is one of the principle keys in Canada's future. It is really ironic. This nation is spending billions of dollars and taking in by revenue billions of dollars, with an export trade the envy of many underdeveloped nations and not a few industrialized nations, with a standard of living, possessed of space, natural resources uncounted and human resources mercifully detached from the problems created by unfriendly neighbours. Yet with all this, with all our achievements, affluence and potential, we must admit to an inability to gainfully employ close to 5 per cent of our people who are able and willing to work.
Surely, the solution to this problem presents challenge enough for the most imaginative and dynamic government. This figure of close to 5 per cent is bad enough, but what is worse is the regional breakdown. Here we find a rate of 7.1 per cent for the Atlantic provinces; 6.8 per cent in Quebec; 3 per cent in Ontario; 3.4 per cent in the Prairies and 5.4 per cent in British Columbia. This is proof positive of the statement of the Economic Council of Canada and I quote:
The level of unemployment in the Atlantic provinces and to a lesser degree Quebec is persistently higher than the national average at all times.
Such a condition points to the need for flexible policies applicable in differing degrees to regional needs, rather than blanket policies which have no regard for regional needs and only accentuate regional disparity. In this regard, we now have the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which will carry on the policy of giving grants to industries to persuade them to establish in certain areas or to stay in areas where they are already established.
What we should have is a very clear picture of how these powers will be applied in this new department and how it will operate. If we were able to spend very large sums of money in the past few years without securing the desired results, let us not repeat that process. If we are going to simply follow the
October 31, 1969

The Address-Mr. Alexander line of least resistance and go Where growth already exists, where industries are already established, then where is the case for this department and its calls for correlation?
The hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau), took this government to task, particularly the Minister of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mar-chand), because there was no liaison between the departments. There is no liaison between that department and the Department of Transport, as well as that of the Postmaster General. The hon. member asked how in heaven's name these slow growth areas are ever to take their place in the main stream of Canadian life when we have ministers who do not even discuss what is going on in terms of relieving the frustrations of the Atlantic provinces.
I am particularly disturbed about the nonrecognition of the complexities of urban growth. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for York North (Mr. Givens) deal briefly with this problem in his speech. It made my heart jump for joy, because I thought I was going to hear a blast against this government that would leave nothing to be desired by the hon. member for York West. This former mayor of Toronto stated that if he were on the treasury benches, he would have ensured that the problems of urban growth would have been included in the Speech from the Throne.
In the 1970's this country will have a population of some 25 million. According to the statistics that have been gathered, the population of this country in the 1980's will be centred in 29 cities. We have heard mention of Toronto and Montreal, and we can even throw in Hamilton. In the next 10 or 15 years Ontario will have a population of 10 million. When we think of these facts we see how significant it is that we should be urban oriented. With all due respect to my rural friends, we have to face the realities.
We have to be concerned about the quality of life being experienced in urban centres. We must be concerned about crime, mental disease, depression, frustration, alcoholism and drug usage. A member of our party stated yesterday the only advice he can give to the youth of our nation today is to "get off the pot". Until such time as I can be shown there is some merit in the use of marijuana and until it is acceptable, I am against it. I also say to the youth of this country, "get off the pot".

We need a recognition that the question of urban growth is one of immediate and profound concern to this nation and to the quality of day to day living in Canada. Yet none of the basic issues of daily life in Canada appears to have moved the imagination of our well-dressed Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or of his less colourful retinue of thinkers, theorists and swingers. In these circumstances, the just society is unobtainable, and its promise is an insult to our intelligence. At the most, it continues to exist as an election slogan which has been almost totally rejected by the farmer, the fisherman, the urban dweller and by the four million of us who are living in poverty today. Let me say, in my own language-and it is language which is becoming increasingly acceptable: this government must stop shafting the poor.
After all, what could we expect? It has been said that the Prime Minister promised
October 31, 1969

nothing. Well, this government, in keeping with that statement has, in the minds of many people, done little or nothing in concrete terms to justify the confidence, plaudits and enthusiasm of Canadians.
In considering the subject of urban renewal we cannot ignore the municipalities. This was made clear by the experience of the government in connection with two airports in particular, one on Toronto Island and the other outside Montreal. The 37th annual conference of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities indicated quite clearly that the Municipalities wished to have a voice in all discussions which concerned urban affairs. These people are concerned about transportation; they are concerned about housing; they want to be brought into discussions at levels upon which their experience can be useful. The Federation expressed a desire to participate whenever possible in the manner set forth at the federal-provincial constitutional conference. If we are to make any headway in this field, we must begin to recognize that because of the rate of urban growth and its increasing complexity we shall have to reach down-and I say that with a great deal of respect-to receive wisdom and guidance from the municipalities.
It has been said that pressures for increased expenditures in urban areas are likely to mount rapidly, and it is to be noted that the real property tax, which is still by far the largest source of local revenue, is considerably less responsive to economic growth than are the revenue sources of the federal and provincial governments. As stated by the Economic Council, the gap between municipal expenditure requirements and the revenue derived by municipalities is likely to increase; in the absence of a continuing increase and transfer of revenue from the senior government or further shifts of responsibility to other levels of government it will become increasingly difficult to maintain, let alone to improve, the quality of the urban environment in which the vast majority of Canadians will be living.
It is extremely important that we become aware of what is happening in terms of urban growth. What about urban renewal? I must have asked 30 or 40 questions on this subject since I came here. We have had a succession of ministers-the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Benson), the former member for Vancouver Centre, Mr. Nicholson, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) and the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras). It seems to me they
The Address-Mr. Alexander each gave consideration to the proper way of approaching urban housing problems and that the municipalities were given every encouragement to pursue the plans which were on their drawing boards. The city of Hamilton was no exception in this regard. It was understood and accepted that its scheme was a good one. The local authority undertook to carry on and the government indicated it was behind this project. It seems to me, now, Mr. Speaker, that Hamilton was led down the garden path and then kicked over the cliff. Hamilton had a $14 million project going in its project for York Street urban renewal and it was looking for some $5 million from the federal government as its contribution. Then, government spokesmen suddenly announced: It's tough luck but we have only $2,500,000.
Do you know what situation has resulted, Mr. Speaker? When I go to York Street today the people who own the stores, shops and homes which have been expropriated ask me what is happening. I say to them: Blame the government in Ottawa.

I shall finish shortly, Mr. Speaker. In order to expedite my remarks I shall read the rest of them, even though my hon. friend in the New Democratic party said that members should learn to speak without the aid of typewritten notes. We will achieve this eventually. You have a new breed of politician in the House now, Mr. Speaker, one who is aware of his functions here and the image that he must project in order that Canadians, as I told some young people here today, will respect this house. I am not afraid that this government will reduce this respect, because it is our function to make sure that this respect continues in the age old tradition of grandeur and understanding.
This government is obsessed with abstract things and has no inclination to tackle the many existing emergencies, some of which I have mentioned. Instead we, as parliamentarians, representing the people of Canada, are asked to treat as urgent matters such as abortion, homosexuality and language rights.
All these may have their importance-there can be no doubt about that; but at the same time it seems to me they should have no priority in a country as urgently in need of action in the economic sector as Canada.
The title of one of the latest reports of the Economic Council of Canada is "Challenge of Growth and Change". This is a challenge that for some reason or another has been continually ducked by this government, even though they continually point out the shortcomings in our economy and what should actually be done to alleviate the many serious situations.
In conclusion, what this country needs is a government that is conscious of the realities. We need a government with policies to alleviate problems resulting from urban growth that are becoming more and more intense. We need a government that can produce instant programs, a government whose first concern is the strengthening of Canada's economy, the

reaffirmation of our national identity and integrity, and the maintenance of Canadian sovereignty within our territories. In this respect, the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with regard to Arctic pollution should have been a little stronger. Let us state firmly that those waters are ours, and then we will see how the cookie crumbles.

Mr. Speaker, may I join in the general acclaim of my colleagues, the hon. members from Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) and Lapointe (Mr. Marceau), who so ably moved and seconded the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. In offering this congratulation I must immediately disclaim any implication of surprise, or even remarkability. The quality of their efforts was really only of that degree of excellence which we in the back rows on both sides and in the rump opposite have come to expect of our parliamentary contemporaries.
Last year when speaking in the budget debate I remarked that the Company of Young Canadians was a controversial creation of Parliament. Certainly, nothing has occurred in recent months to cause me to amend that assessment. The Company is currently under assault by some of the most influential political figures in Canada. The Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts has now been charged with the responsibility of looking into its operation. In view of the tenor of some of the charges giving rise to this investigation, one might almost expect the national defence committee to have been given this responsibility.
However, I am extremely happy that a subcommittee of that committee, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Osier), will be visiting Calgary to hear evidence on C.Y.C. activities there. Whatever the situation elsewhere, they will have the opportunity to review a C.Y.C. operation that has worked and worked well; an operation that has, with the very limited means available to it, fulfilled its function of bridging the gap between the mainstream of society and some of its alienated elements, and left behind it a residue of ongoing community leadership. It is an operation which, in short, has achieved the objectives its creators visualized.
There are a number of recently, and perhaps temporarily, unemployed politicians in Calgary who must regret profoundly their assessment that the repercussions of C.Y.C.

The Address-Mr. Mahoney activity there was a cause, rather than a symptom, of civic malaise.
I had the honour early this month, at the invitation of the Canadian Institute of International Affairs, to attend and participate in a seminar sponsored by the John F. Kennedy Institute for Atlantic Studies at the University of Tilburg in The Netherlands. The subject of the seminar was NATO and security in the seventies. Following this I visited, along with other members of this chamber and the other place, the Council of Europe at Strasbourg; the First Canadian Air Division at Lahr, and the Fourth Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group on manoeuvres in the field near Brunswick, Germany.
I then took part with the parliamentary delegation in the deliberations of the North Atlantic Assembly in Brussels, and with a smaller group representing this Parliament at a meeting in Paris under the auspices of the development aid committee of the Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development. This latter meeting focussed its attention on the report on development aid entitled "Partners in Development" prepared for the World Bank by a distinguished committee under the chairmanship of our immediate past Prime Minister, the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson.
I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie) who headed our delegation to Brussels. The preparation and advance briefing that we received was extremely valuable, and this was carrying on the tradition established last year by the hon. Senator John Aird. I sincerely hope that this tradition of briefing and preparing of delegations, and of establishing a degree of continuity between parliamentary delegations to the more important international assemblies, will be continued.
[DOT] (3:0C p.m.)
There is no doubt in my mind, in the mind of any informed European, or in the minds of our troops in Europe, that our soldiers are, man for man, the finest, best trained and most effective military force on that continent. They are professionals. They are capable of fulfilling their assigned task better than any other force, but that capability does not necessarily mean that the assigned task is the right task; and just because it was the right task 15, 10, or even five years ago does not mean it is necessarily the right task now. An uncritical perpetuation of the existing role would be tantamount to closing our eyes to some very fundamental changes in the balance of world power.
October 31, 1989

The Address-Mr. Mahoney
There is the greatly increased capacity of the European nations to provide for their own defence in conventional terms. There is the awareness that an incident in the European theatre likely to escalate into any sort of war-the so-called accident-will more likely occur on one of NATO's lightly guarded flanks, Norway, Turkey, the Mediterranean, rather than in the relatively heavily armed centre, Germany where any action would almost immediately bring the aggressors into contact with United States troops and a possible nuclear retaliation. There is the fact that on a global basis the United States and Russia have achieved practical parity in the capacity for mutual obliteration by strategic nuclear weapons. There is the fact of growing Chinese power and ever-increasing ferment in the developing world. There is the evident thrust of Soviet policy to compete with the United States as a global military power. This is implicit in the growing show of Soviet naval strength particularly in the Mediterranean but also in the Indian and Atlantic Oceans. It is implicit in the development of the Antonov 22 long-range, troop transport aircraft, the helicopter carriers now at sea or nearing completion, and the expansion of their marine infantry.
Russia is rapidly equipping itself to perform the same global role of which the United States is presently capable. Once it has this capability, and given de facto strategic nuclear equality with the United States, will Russia be able to avoid involvement in distant trouble spots? Is it not likely that opportunities for involvement will be more numerous than in the past?
Canada's defence policy, with the pre-eminent position given its NATO commitment, was formulated before these fundamental changes in the balance of world power at a time when one could with reasonable certainty postulate that the only real peril to Canada was the fact that a nuclear war between Russia and the United States would necessarily involve us; that the most likely cause of such a war would arise in Europe and that Canada's interests were, therefore, best served by a total commitment to NATO. With changing conditions the only real peril to Canada remains, for the time being at least, the fact that a nuclear war between Russia and the United States will necessarily involve us. But we can no longer safely assume that Europe is the only place where a confrontation leading to that war is likely to occur; indeed, it seems more likely to occur elsewhere.
The situation which we face justifies the decision to rearrange our defence priorities and it also justifies the reconfiguration-that is the official word, not mine-which will see integrated, highly mobile air transportable troops forming the basic fighting units of our armed forces. But while the transformation of, if you like, reconfiguration may be the right thing to do, it will not be an inexpensive thing to do. Concern must be expressed that the current economy drive could seriously impair and even delay this process at a time when it is vital that it proceed with all due dispatch. Given adequate resources our Canadian armed forces will continue to be, man for man, the free world's most effective military force, filling an even more valuable role than in the past. A second element of our foreign policy, development aid, is receiving increased attention, and indeed has been exempted from the expenditure guidelines which the government has applied to practically all other areas of activity. This attitude of the Canadian government is somewhat unique in the international community today.
The first pages of the Pearson Commission Report are replete with such terms as "feasibility in question", "disillusion and distrust", "volume stagnant", "commitments declining", "spirit of disenchantment", "misconceptions", "criticism of waste" and "frustration and impatience". The report acknowledges that international support for development is now flagging. Recognition of this fact led the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development to call together last week parliamentarians from countries which are members of its Development Aid Committee. This invitation was unprecedented in the history of the OECD which has tended in the past to conduct its affairs quietly and with dignity at the official and ministerial levels, a rather natural reflection of the fact that the OECD is the rich man's club of the global village.
Its member countries account for 61 per cent of the world's industrial production and 65 per cent of world trade, while containing but 20 per cent of its population. They also disburse 90 per cent of its development aid. They called in parliamentarians because they recognize that they are going to have a tough time selling a maintenance, much less an increase, in development aid over the next few years. The Pearson Report enumerates clearly not only what development aid can do but what it cannot and should not be expected to do. At this particular time of disenchantment, a definition of misconceptions is

Ociober 31. 1969	COMMONS
probably as important as a definition of potential.
Development will not guarantee a choice of a particular ideology or value system; nor political stability nor rejection of violence; nor peaceful and responsible international behaviour; nor will it buy dependable friends. So why bother? Of course, there are moral reasons; the feeling that it is right for the "haves" to share with the "have nots". There is the appeal of enlightened self-interest, a somewhat shopworn expression which embraces the concept that improved utilization of the world's resources will benefit the rich as well as the poor. Most important is the fact that we live in a global village; that a war anywhere may affect us all; that pollution in one area may affect the entire world; that pestilence does not stop at national boundaries. In brief, there is no way of knowing where Canada or any other country will be next year, 10 years or 100 years from now, unless we can also know where the world will be. If we want to be secure and prosperous we must try to ensure that the world is secure and prosperous.
One of the more significant phenomena in western Europe today is that of the growing irrelevance of national boundaries. For over a decade young people-and not all of them are still young-have been moving freely from Naples to Oslo and from Munich to Dublin. They recognize themselves as Europeans, not Dutchmen or Danes. This phenomenon is spreading throughout many parts of the world. It has crossed the Atlantic; it has penetrated the iron curtain. There is among the young a conviction that we are a world community and that we must behave like a world community if we are to survive as a civilization. The concept of world community is itself a compelling reason for development aid. Development aid is an act of faith in the future. The poorer nations have made their choice. They intend to develop. The questions are how fast and at what cost. Developed nations can speed their progress and ease their way.
The Pearson Report also tells the story of the first development decade and outlines a strategy for the second. The record of the first is better by far than most of us appreciate. The average rate of increase of gross national product in the developing countries has reached 5 per cent per annum, although the population explosion has held the annual per capita rate to 2J per cent. Remember, these are gross averages. Some individual countries have done much better than average, others

The Address-Mr. Mahoney have remained relatively stagnant, while yet others-Indonesia and Uruguay, for example-have actually experienced per capita declines.
However much the western wheat farmer may regret the loss of markets, he must rejoice in the conquest of starvation in many parts of the world as the green revolution gains momentum. However much the textile industry may resent competitive pressures, it must be grateful for the options that are open to its owners and workers in Canada, few of which are open in the developing world.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
School enrolment has almost tripled, although the tools and techniques are too often antiquated and the education too often classical rather than technical, with no suitable productive job waiting for the student. Public health conditions have improved immeasurably, resulting directly in lower mortality, higher birth rates and often critical unemployment and underemployment. The results and experience of the first development decade indicate a need for massive research if the second decade is to produce optimum results.
The amount spent on development aid will not be the only, nor even necessarily the most important, criterion in determining its value. Its form can be vital, as can the purposes for which it is spent. Its effectiveness in stimulating economic growth will be the critical measure. It is, therefore, not surprising that this government's decision to create a Canadian International Development Research Centre, announced in the Throne Speech and followed by introduction and first reading of the bill this Wednesday, is greeted with unqualified enthusiasm throughout the world. Only through research can we contemplate the possibility of optimum value in development assistance.
Mr. Speaker, there are strong indications that a very important segment of the American people are becoming preoccupied with their grave domestic problems. There was little doubt in the minds of the United States congressmen attending the North Atlantic Assembly in Brussels that, barring some unforeseen circumstance, substantial numbers of their troops would be returned to the United States from Europe. Most of the Europeans I spoke to regarded this as inevitable, if regrettable. Outspoken United States proponents of development aid hold forth little hope that the United States will increase its program; indeed, many expect further
October 31, 1963

The Address-Mr. Mahoney reductions. And yet this is no time tor policies to become introverted.
A few days ago I received a letter from a constituent, a CPR employee who had discovered to his dismay that while pension credit would be given to him for time served in either World War I or World War II, no such credit would be granted for Korea. This led me to do a little research. The CPR is technically correct. It may come as a surprise to many-it did to me-that ever since September 2, 1945, when some 500 miles northeast of the smouldering ruins of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan surrendered unconditionally to the allies, the world has been at peace. There has not been a war any place in the world for over 24 years. Not a single war has been declared. Mind you, there have been some 50 conflicts since 1945 that could be graced by the appellation "war" had the traditional formalities been observed. Sixteen of these have been fought between sovereign states; others have been anti-colonial uprisings and civil wars, and in about half of these foreign troops have been involved.
The Korean conflict was not a war. It went under the name of a police action even though soldiers of 24 countries were involved. Almost two million soldiers and uncounted civilians were casualties and three years of gigantic military effort was expended. War was never declared and it never ended. The fighting stopped, not with a formal surrender but with an inconclusive armistice that has yet to be ratified. Today, patrols still clash and the Armistice Commission still meets to exchange insults. Wars do not begin and wars do not end any more; they just kind of happen and they are happening at numerous street corners in our global village today-the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Nigeria. There is still the occasional rumble in Korea and the Kashmir.
As citizens of this global village, neither Canadians nor Americans can divorce themselves from what goes on outside our particular block. We must continue to direct our efforts outward and to avail ourselves of every means at our disposal to improve our village. Notwithstanding the seriousness and immediacy of our own domestic problems, we simply cannot afford to become recluse. Development aid may be fairly regarded as the international equivalent of an enlightened domestic social development program, a program to give the less advantaged in a community the opportunity to share equitably in the benefits of living there.

Nowhere has the most enlightened social program yet devised by man produced conditions which have permitted a community-national, municipal or otherwise-to disband its police force. Nothing in human experience to date indicates that the most enlightened development aid program will justify the entire, or even substantial elimination of armed forces. While we may hope it will, we cannot safely anticipate that result.
I cannot find a better way to sum up my feelings than to repeat one sentence from the Throne Speech:
Our world has become so compact, so Interdependent, that all humanity is wounded by an outbreak of violence in any corner of the earth.
That is a compelling reason for implementing and maintaining an effective development aid program. It is equally a compelling reason for maintaining effective military forces. Acceptance of this fact is a sound base upon which to build foreign and defence policies which could be the models for free and prosperous nations having no ambitions but to live in an increasingly free and increasingly prosperous world.

As for the average Canadian, he concludes that practically no efficient measure has yet been taken to cope with the increasing poverty in this country. This is a serious problem, which spreads panic and poverty, sometimes dire poverty, in homes that are entitled to more consideration on the part of our governments.
And why, Mr. Speaker, is there so much unemployment in my riding? Mostly because the plants are up against the unfavourable competition of goods imported from countries where the salaries paid the workers are much lower than those the Canadian industries have to pay.

The Address-Mr. Ricard foreign competition. I do not want to exaggerate but, if my information is correct-and I believe it is-another plant in St. Hyacinthe will fold soon, which is certainly no cause for rejoicing.

I was recently provided with information about the Canadian electronics industry. That industry is faced with difficulties for several reasons, mainly because of competition from foreign products. The Canadian electronics industry provides jobs for approximately 60,000 Canadians. During the year 1968, it exported abroad $300 million worth of merchandise. It is now handicapped and finds it very difficult to meet foreign competition, for excise tax at the rate of 15 per cent has to be paid in addition to the 12 per cent sales tax. Such charges leave it almost helpless to fight those countries that deprive it of its natural market here in Canada.
Moreover, the tariff reduction under the Kennedy Round to become effective in 1972 only came into force last June. The Canadian manufacturers find themselves at a disadvantage because they have to pay higher sales and excise taxes than importers. In the interest of Canadian manufacturers and workers this situation should be corrected as soon as possible.
Some industries would like to settle in the St-Hyacinthe region, but they are not doing so on account of the unfavourable position in which they find themselves due to the fact that this region is considered to be part of the Montreal region. As it is not in a designated area, the city of St. Hyacinthe cannot avail itself of the advantages given to the so-called designated regions. To my knowledge there are at least two very important industries which would have preferred to settle in St. Hyacinthe where serious, skilful and stable manpower is to be found, but because of the drawbacks resulting from the fact that the St. Hyacinthe region is not recognized as a designated area, they went elsewhere.

The Address-Mr. Ricard
Believe it or not, but St. Hyacinthe has been included in the Montreal area. In the opinion of those responsible for designating areas, St. Hyacinthe has the same characteristics as Montreal.
