speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to have the opportunity of speaking during this debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. Having read or heard the various speeches made by hon. members since the debate began, I wish to say that the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne did themselves proud on the opening day of the session.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
There are several items 1 would like to raise this afternoon, but like other hon. members of the House I feel I must be critical of what is a lack of proper direction by the present administration and a lack of concrete programming policy for the solution of the many problems which face Canada today. Last year we were giving the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government an opportunity to find their feet and outline a program. We hoped that with the start of this new session of parliament we would have something a little more concrete than what w:e received on opening day.
I point out that we in the opposition should review quite frequently the program and the progress made by the present administration. This brings home to them and the Canadian people the fact which must be crystal clear to an ever-increasing group of Canadians, that all our problems are not being solved. It is not as though this administration has not
[Mr. Ricard.)
DEBATES	October 31, 1969
been in power for a sufficient period of tune in which to take action to solve some of our problems. It came into power in April of 1963, although I frankly admit they did not have a majority government until June of 1968, when our present Prime Minister headed the administration. We all recall rather vividly the campaign of 16 months ago when the cry of a "just society" rang from the Atlantic to the Pacific and the people of this nation felt that here was a Moses come to lead us to the promised land.
Many of the major issues which faced us prior to the election in 1968 are far more serious now than they were when this administration took office 16 months ago. The disturbing factor is that solutions to many of the problems have not been offered by the government. I believe it is fair to say that from all appearances this government does not have a program or a solution to many of the major problems facing us. We hear a lot of talk about inflation, which I think is the No. 1 problem facing Canada today. The government tried to solve this problem by cutting back expenditures. This caused more unemployment than we should have in our nation. They have been singularly unsuccessful in reducing the alarming rise in inflation which is facing this nation. In fact, over the past year the rate of increase has accelerated, not decreased. This is an indication the government must be on the wrong track.
The result of the current program by which the government has been attempting to fight the inflationary pressures and trends in this country has meant several things to the Canadian people. I mentioned earlier there was a sharp increase in unemployment. Today it stands at roughly 5 per cent, which is far too high for this time of year. In addition, we find that a very sharp incomes restraint and a reduction in living standards through inflation have placed an additional burden on the backs of pensioners, veterans and welfare recipients. The government has told these people it is not good to increase pensions; they cannot afford to increase the veteran's basic pay because of the inflationary tendencies it would cause.
This government has taken other steps such as releasing many civil servants. One of the most unfortunate cutbacks ever made was the unfair blow dealt to civil servants, especially those in the older age brackets, when the government indicated that people in their 60's would be retired from the service. All that these civil servants have done is grow old; they have reached the age of 60 or a little
October 31, 19G9	COMMONS
more. The government decided to take action by retiring them when they could least afford to retire, perhaps at a time when they had accumulated debts which they had to meet out of salaries which they expected to receive over a number of years. I fail to see how this method of dealing with civil servants falls into that of a just society.
I wish to spend a few moments dealing with unemployment. I mentioned earlier that the unemployment rate is now 5 per cent of the labour force, on a seasonally adjusted basis. Forecasts for the coming winter months indicate that it will be an extremely grim time. I do not think there is any doubt that we will see a sharp increase in the unemployment rate all across Canada. There have been forecasts of an unemployment rate amounting to between 7 and 8 per cent, and in some areas which are less favoured economically it is possible that the rate will be 10 per cent. Yet we have received a warning from the Economic Council of Canada over the years that 3 per cent is the limit Canada can afford to carry. The rate has been running much higher than that; in fact, in some instances it has been twice as high. Members on all sides will agree with me that even normal unemployment is wasteful enough because of the tremendous loss of productivity it entails as well as the harmful social effect upon those who suffer from it. Unemployment brought about through the action of the government amounts, in my opinion, to utter stupidity, the more so because it has completely failed in its objective of checking inflation.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Last year the government indicated it was eliminating the winter works program which had been used fairly effectively-at least in my part of the country-by many of the municipalities to ease their winter unemployment rate. We were told at the time that retraining programs would replace the winter works program. In fact, we found that the retraining program covered only a small portion of the unemployed. It was just another example of "too little and too late". Retraining programs are excellent, but more is required; something else must go hand in hand with them. Jobs must be available for those who have acquired new skills, or the retraining is merely a futile and expensive exercise. We have had examples in various parts of the country of cases in which retrained workmen have been unable to obtain jobs.
I should like to deal briefly with the effects of inflation on the incomes and living standards of those receiving fixed incomes. This
DEBATES	383
The Address-Mr. Harding has always been a problem, one which has upset members in every part of this House. It applies particularly to pensioners of all descriptions, to veterans and to welfare recipients. The government has taken no adequate action to even maintain the purchasing power of these groups over the years. As a result they see their meagre and inadequate purchasing power further declining.
In this age of affluence every Canadian-should share in the increasing productivity of the nation. No group, particularly when it includes those who cannot bargain effectively for themselves, should be denied an adequate income. The failure of the government to maintain even the present purchasing power of their fixed incomes is another sure sign that the just society is merely a political phrase used to attract voters at election time. The rapidly rising cost of living over the years has made it imperative that basic pension rates be increased and that a cost of living clause be built into them so as at least to maintain the purchasing power of pensions. Those who helped to build this Canada of ours are surely entitled to share in the ever-increasing prosperity of our nation.
The recent government white paper on veterans pensions must have come as a shock to veterans organizations and to veterans in every part of Canada. As a result of the recommendation of the Woods Committee we had hoped to see adequate increases in basic pensions. This did not materialize. It is another example of the failure of the government to deal adequately with the social needs of this group. Again, the government blames inflation for depriving our veterans of a long awaited improvement in their pension position. I could go on in this vein; there are a host of similar questions which could be raised.
The government has proved altogether inadequate in its handling of the housing situation. I shall not go more deeply into that subject this afternoon because time will not permit. There is one matter I should like to raise in connection with the affairs of my own riding. It concerns air transportation. I raise it this afternoon feeling that in this modern age when air transportation has become so important to every section of our country, effective communication by air is vital to economic and social development.
When one sees air transportation facilities going downhill, and when one finds that air transportation authorities are unable to deal effectively with the situation, I believe the matter must be raised again and again until
384	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Harding something is done. I am aware that the Air Transport Committee is looking into the question of air travel in the southern section of British Columbia, but I am not happy about some of the steps it has taken. While airlines on trans-Atlantic routes are reducing their rates we find the commission authorizing increases in my area of up to 30 per cent, even though the service has been cut to a point which is harmful to the needs of those who will use it.
All this makes me wonder what type of planning is going on in the various departments of government. How many letters does one have to write, how many telephone calls does one have to make, how many individuals does one have to visit before it becomes clear that an area has been harmed? The initial planning done by the Air Transport Committee in this connection was poor; it was ineffective and it has hurt the area. I believe a review should be initiated without delay and that a better service should be granted to the area. We are approaching the '70s when air transportation will be one of the keys to economic success, and we cannot afford to see this service go downhill.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I should now like to make a few observations in connection with pollution. I intend to speak somewhat generally, because time will not permit me to cover all the points I should like to raise this afternoon. Members of all parties are extremely interested in pollution. I am very happy to see the newspapers and various news media giving more and more coverage to pollution problems as they arise. Pollution has become one of the major issues facing not only the federal government but all levels of government in Canada. Indeed, it is a major problem facing all nations.
A few years ago we thought that our fresh waters and oceans were so vast that we could not possibly pollute them. We thought our atmosphere was limitless and could not possibly be polluted. We thought our resources of land so extensive that we could not pollute them. We thought the ecology of this world was so varied and diverse that mere man could do little to harm it. We have gone merrily along, ignoring the danger signs, until today we find mankind has imperilled its very existence on this planet. The history of this earth is full of accounts of animal species and civilizations that became extinct because they could not adapt themselves to changing conditions. This is fact. Today the picture is different. We are slowly but surely laying

DEBATES	October 31. 1969
systematic waste to our environment, and unless we make some radical changes, and make them quickly, we will do irreparable harm.
Even people in Canada are becoming pollution conscious. Perhaps a series of world-wide pollution disasters has alerted us to the danger. For example, Mr. Speaker, within the past few months we have learned of the poisoning of the Rhine River. There were stories in the newspapers and on television about the millions of fish that were poisoned. The water supply of millions of people was endangered. The cause was finally traced to two barrels of insecticide that had fallen unnoticed off a river barge two years previously. These barrels had remained on the river bed until they rusted open and brought their death-dealing poisons to all living organisms in the river.
There was a very fine editorial in the Vancouver Province outlining several areas where nations of the world have dumped surplus and obsolete supplies of possibly dangerous pollutants into various parts of our vast oceans. Nations had no previous experience of the damage that could be done to the ecology of the oceans, yet vast supplies of waste material were just dumped.
For example, the United States has dumped thousands of containers of obsolete second world war nerve gas off the New Jersey coast. They do not know how long it will take for these containers to rust through; perhaps it will take a century, maybe two, maybe less. When the containers do rust through, no one knows the result that this injection of poison into the ocean will have ecologically. The British and the French are reported to have dumped chemical warfare agents off their coasts. There is a report that in Sweden a gold mining company prior to the last world war dumped many containers of arsenic into the Baltic Sea. It is estimated there is enough poison in these containers to kill all life in the Baltic. Some day these containers will rust through, the arsenic will seep into the water and mankind will be hard put to finding a solution to a man-made problem that should never have been allowed to arise. More recently we have had the example of poison-gas being dumped off an island in the Pacific by the Japanese, and today conditions on the island are unlivable. Such incidents as these are examples of foolishness on the part of governments that are trying to get rid of what they consider to be obsolete supplies.
In addition to this we pour gas and filth into our air at an astounding rate. Reports from Los Angeles indicate the seriousness of
Ociober 31, 1969	COMMONS
the air pollution problem there. Officials in Los Angeles have announced a program cancelling physical education activity in schools in the area when the smog count reaches a certain level. This level is attained at least 21 times a year. Studies indicate that the children suffer lung damage during heavy physical activity undertaken in such conditions. Smog conditions not as serious as in Los Angeles exist in all major cities in this country, and every year we add to air pollution. An American, Dr. Sternglass, after years of research has claimed that the result of nuclear fallout, even of minor amounts, has been far more devastating than previously expected. His work on infant mortality and its relation to fallout is both revealing and disturbing.
I should like to spend a few minutes on another aspect of pollution, the use of DDT and detergents. In the event that I am unable to complete my remarks on both, I shall deal with the problem of detergents first. A pollution study of the Great Lakes was made in 1965 for the International Joint Commission. The report, which has recently come to hand, indicates that the most serious aspect of detergent pollution is the use of phosphorous in detergents. We are all aware that phosphorous helps nourish the algae which choke the waters of the Great Lakes system. The report points out that 50 to 70 per cent of the phosphorous in this fresh water supply area comes from detergents. The recommendation of the report is that the use of phosphorous by detergent manufacturers should be banned within the next two years. The point that worries me is this. We in Canada have carried out no study or research into this question. I think we should have done so in past years.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
We might say that we can rely a great deal on what is done to the south of us because in the United States they are doing far more research than we are. However, in reply to questions asked in this House, various ministers have indicated there is today no danger in the use of DDT as far as Canada is concerned.

Unemployment is an insult to human dignity, and so is an impersonal welfare system. It is also an indignity to provide insufficient protection to our citizens against criminal activities. Every Canadian should feel proud of himself in the presence of his children and his neighbours and he should be able to rely on every level of the government in this respect. Canadian society does not have an overflow of skills; we cannot therefore afford to waste the smallest contribution that each individual can bring to the country.
One must admit that the present situation is not what it should be.
Our economy is not what it should be. It is stagnating and off balance. Cullen and Marceau) of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne.
It is said that we should upgrade our strength. That we should do more for society, that we should expand our efforts so that our talents do not go astray-this is what the Prime Minister said-and the Minister of Finance wants to stand in the way of all that when he says:
I have said before and I repeat that the number one problem we face in this country today is the persistent upward spiral in prices, costs and incomes. Other than this, we have a prosperous and viable economy. However, unless and until we bring this spiral of inflation under effective control, all the aspirations of this house toward a better life for all Canadians, all our hopes for continuous high employment, for a rising standard of living and justice for the poor and the depressed in our country, will come to nought.
But why do we experience that spiral of inflation in peace time while we never experienced any in war time? That is what I will try to explain.

The Address-Mr. Latulippe
How is it that in Russia, a communist country, there is no inflation? In Canada, we cannot balance our economy in order to settle this problem and due to that inflationary spiral, we keep on making many rich people richer and 80 per cent of the people poorer. Twenty per cent of the people are responsible for inflation and I will say at once that our chartered banks have increased their assets by $6,600 million in one year, which is twice the value of the bank notes issued by the Bank of Canada since 1934, that is since its institution 35 years ago.
Never have the banks made such profits, and not only the banks but other lending institutions which lend money at rates ranging from 10 to 20 per cent. Those institutions are the ones which make profits and create inflation, while the cost of inflation is borne by those who are laid flat, that is 80 per cent of the Canadian population. Because of credit restrictions and rising interest rates of every kind, they can no longer carry on. And they are being asked to pay the cost of inflation.
At the hearings of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, I met the Governor of the Bank of Canada and asked him a question. He was saying that Canadians had been prosperous long enough and that this should cease. But why has prosperity lasted long enough? According to him, Canadians had to tighten their belts to settle the problem of inflation. Then I asked him how come his $50,000 salary had been raised to $75,000? Why had every senior official of the government enjoyed similar increases while the people of Canada had to tighten their belts? The senior officials however loosen theirs. It is quite all right for them to have increases in salaries, increases here, increases there, not to mention expenses paid.
The people have a right to live, for they are the ones who work, who build the country; and not just the executive class.
The government is not producing anything; it is only ensuring the administration and if it is not capable of administering a country that is crammed with riches, where wheat is plentiful, if it cannot succeed in giving the population what they are entitled to, then it might as well resign, because it is a poor manager. That is what we have in parliament and within the Public Service: senior civil servants who are incapable of finding another solution to the problem besides increasing taxes, the cost of living, the interest rates, thus enriching a small part of the population and impoverishing the rest.


This cannot last much longer. We know of much dissatisfaction in Canada. We witness all sorts of phenomenons that we have never seen in the past. We see deplorable strikes. There is dissatisfaction, riots because the people have not got what they are entitled to.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The people are unfortunately no longer able to get the necessities of life without having to kneel before the big financiers and borrow money bearing an interest rate of 15 or 20 per cent. It is impossible to do anything without incurring debts that cannot be repaid, that remain forever. That is the situation which we must bring to an end.
Although the Canadian economy is still the most flourishing in the world, as the Minister of Finance said, although generally speaking the capitalist economy, that of the free enterprise, is still inferior to that of socialism or communism, I maintain, and I have evidence to prove it, that the Canadian economy, our capitalistic, free enterprise economy, involves certain basic deficiencies like inflation, the rise in the cost of living, interest rates, unemployment, numerous strikes, which are only visible symptoms appearing at certain times and at certain places.
The basic weakness of our economy, the only source of all the ailments afflicting our economy today is the increase in interest rates. This single cause of our numerous economic ailments stems from the very core of Canada's capitalist, free-enterprise economy. It would be very easy to eliminate it. Nothing indeed would be easier than restoring the balance between the various elements which constitute our economy.
Be it in any country of the world, subject to any political regime, be it capitalism, socialism or communism, everywhere on our planet, which is called Earth, there are natural ressources. Indeed, it is easy to see that everywhere people cultivate, work, produce, consume, save, finance.
Everywhere healthy adults must carry the onus of production for all the citizens in the world at large including those who are either too young, too old, too sick or too uneducated to earn a living in a society whose duty is to protect them.
In 1969 here in Canada, with the output of 8 million adult citizens, with their capital and labour we have a gross national product of 72 billion for the benefit of 21 million Canadians, including 13 million people too young, too old,
Ociober 31, 1969	COMMONS
too sick or too uneducated too look after themselves in our capitalistic society of free enterprise.
If we divide $72 billion by 21 million citizens we get an annual per capita product of $3,400, or $17,000 for a family of five. Further computations would give us an amount of $65 per week and per person, or $325 for a family of five. I quote those figures for the benefit of our economists who love to base their estimations on averages.
Such figures are very encouraging and such a high G.N.P. is amply sufficient for the 21 million Canadians to be reasonably well off, while enabling the most qualified and most deserving citizens to maintain their income level and enjoy decent wages.
If our national product is so good, what are we complaining about? Let us not be poetical and vague. I will not beat around the bush. I shall mention our problems and our troubles, but, more particularly, I shall search for their causes and suggest a few solutions. Is this not logical, is this not what we all want?
The problem does not lie in a lack of production, but rather in an imbalance in its distribution. This is the basis of all economic troubles which are undermining our national, family and personal life.
Whether we like it or not, our country has 21 million inhabitants, 8 million of whom are producers as a result of their capital and their work and 13 million of whom have no capital income whatsoever. Those 21 million Canadians have the right to draw on the national product of $72 billion, which we owe to the 8 million producing Canadians who get wages for their work and interests for their capital. In the production of goods and services, there are expenses for wages, labour, and capital interests.
Every time the wages of workers are raised and every time capitalists increase their interest rates, the 8 million producing citizens, as well as the 13 million non producing Canadians automatically have to pay more for goods and services.
Here is the basic weakness of our Canadian economy of the capitalist, free enterprise type. Productive citizens have an income resulting from their work and assets, which constitute for them a purchasing power, while 13 million non-productive citizens, unemployed and witout any income, depend on the productive citizens.
All our economists, politicians, administrators and university teachers have refused to

The Address-Mr. Latulippe date to analyse this simple matter of the income of the individual, of the citizen in relation with his right to live, and everybody wants to consider only the value of work and capital in terms of production as a source of income giving the right to national production.
Instead of carrying on so much research and so many inquiries into the apparent ills of our economy, poverty, inflation, strikes, unemployment, the cost of living, the increase in interest rates, let us go directly to the heart of the matter. Let us hasten to put some order in the Canadian economy between its various components, and at the same time, we will have resolved all the problems that can be summed up by a lack of balance between the incomes, expenditures and profits of all citizens, families, and corporations that need to be better managed.
Whether we like it or not, whether we realize it or not, with all due respect to Mr. Keynes, there is only one normal administrative formula, whatever the importance of the organization to be administered: it is the formula "Incomes-Expenditures-Profits". One formula for all. Let us not look for any other, because I think nobody will be able to find one.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Every company needs revenues to pay its expenses, make some profit and build a reserve for its development and security. Every private or public company, every community, church, school, university, bank, industry, business or farm needs revenues to its operating and other expenses, make a little profit and provide for its development and security. All accountants are fully aware of that, so long as they deal with their own business or that of their companies, their institutions or the people they are responsible for.
Mr. Speaker, the same formula: "revenues, expenses, profits", the sole capitalist formula, valid everywhere, applies just as well and perhaps even better to the private citizens and their families, to the farmers and the small personal and family enterprises.
Indeed, this same income-expense-profit formula is also needed for the 13 million Canadians who have the right to live in Canada. Even if they do not derive any income from their work or their investments, they all have the right to live in Canada in 1969 on the national production of $72 billion made possible by the 8 million Canadians who are paid for their work and are receiving interest on their capital.
October 31, 1969

The Address-Mr. Latulippe
Let us not try to produce any more or to make bigger profits until we have restored national economic equality among people, families, corporations and re-established a balance between incomes, expenses and profits. All have a right to derive some income from the national production which should prove sufficient to cover their expenses and even to get a little profit, build some reserve, security, capital for themselves, their family or the community.
Everybody can see that I am more of a capitalist than a creditiste. I am not asking for credit or for income, but I am asking for money, for capital. I want to make that quite clear. It is easy to see that I am much more of a capitalist than all the members put together.
I am in favour of profit, of higher income and in favour of citizens, but what I want for myself, for businesses, for companies, for municipalities, for provinces or for the country, I also want it in equal proportions for every Canadian citizen, for every Canadian family.
This is what administration is all about. This is the way to run things. This is the stand we should take, how we must develop our human feelings and also, how we must work to balance our economy which is so much out of balance that the more we apply it, the more we unbalance our system, the more we disrupt to our economy.
Here is the basis of our capitalism. The formula which is so good, so promising, so stimulating for all those who are engaged in setting up private or state enterprises, must be as promising and stimulating for every citizen and family which make up the population of Canada.
In the present circumstances, it is essential to realize that it is not a matter of raising or reducing interest rates on capital, of increasing or lowering salaries in proportion to work, but simply of determining whether to balance the national economy among its various constitutive elements.
Poverty, unemployment, recessions, inflation, wars, revolutions, separatism, protest, higher cost of living, higher interest rates, higher taxes, unemployment insurance, old age pensions, allowances, welfare benefits, all those things obviously indicate a lack of balance in the distribution of a overly large national production.
We are so rich that nobody should be without the necessaries and even luxuries in Canada.

This inward and subconscious feeling of every right-minded citizen seeks to express itself in some way or other through various intellectual, aggressive and even violent means, when the authorities have turned a deaf ear to reasonable arguments and advice.
Let us stop raising interest rates. This is of no consequence at the present time. The inflation will persist until order and balance are restored on the national level among all the components of our national economy, beginning with the individual, the family and all the public and private corporations which make up our Canadian nation.
Is that project not comforting? Is it not the best? Would one rather have a small part of the people experience inflation while most of them would be subject to deflation? Until we decide to throw everything out and to start anew, from scratch, as happened in Russia in 1917, we must apply everywhere and as soon as possible our capitalistic formula: Income -Expenses-Profits, for the benefit of individuals, families and companies.
I would have several things to say, but I shall go on attempting to demonstrate that our economy is far from balanced. Our economy is far from satisfying our citizens.
You only have to use your head to know what it is all about. For example, how is it that a world which seemed almost feverishly prosperous in 1929, capable of offering an affluence of commodities and services, became poverty-stricken in 1930? That apparent change was so fundamental that economic conditions were drastically changed.
Is it reasonable to imagine that, between a certain day of October 1929 and a few months later, the world really went from great riches to dire poverty? Yet, the soil has never refused to bend under the plow and produce.
How is it that after knowing scarce money for ten years, all of a sudden, overnight, the necessary funds were found to wage a war which lasted six years and cost billions of dollars? Many of you are aware of this.
After the war, why did we fail at the same task? We were unable to avoid other recessions and the unemployment they create simply because, once again, we tried to fool around with monetary policies based on a system which creates bank debts. Since confederation, this same bank system has never given other results than the repetition of cycles-prosperity in wartime, recession in peacetime.
The first goal of our Canadian economy must be to increase the standard of living of
October 31. 1969

Canadians, as much as possible, through the full use of our manpower and our natural resources. It is unfairly impossible to try to reach that goal with a banking system under which money, created out of nothing in a proportion of 96 per cent in Canada, is being circulated in the form of an interest-bearing debt, which compels us to reimburse more money that has been issued.
We will never reach that goal with a banking system the prime purpose of which is to make money and by forcing the borrowers to repay both the money loaned and the interests, owing to that ineffable conspiration born of the madness of finance.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
This objective can only be reached by creating a banking system and a banking policy that will ensure a constant flow of money or a sufficient purchasing power not only for producing all possible goods in keeping with our human and natural resources, but also for making feasible the distribution of our national production or its equivalent.
I would very much like to know why the governments, Liberal as well as Conservative, have always refused so far to amend the Bank Act and to require Parliament to issue at cost at least part of the currency which the country needs as far as the public sector is concerned. In the past, governments have failed to assume their responsibilities by granting private institutions the exclusive right to issue credit money which is 90 per cent of our economic machinery.
Therefore, money is in short supply while production is potentially high enough to meet normal human needs and if money starts flowing when producers and production facilities are requisitioned by the military, that is because the present monetary system forces decisions on us instead of simply reflecting the free acts of free producers and consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with my colleagues in congratulating the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne.
The Address-Mr. Breau

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the hon. member for Sarnia (Mr. Cullen) that I share his concern for the relevancy of this house. Sometimes we find that Canadians have a hard time understanding why parliament is not more relevant.

Mr. Speaker, it is comforting indeed to see members from the province of Quebec, like the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau), express so proudly in this house their satisfaction at being a part of the Canadian Confederation. I believe the separatist element in Quebec has become a political fact and that it is at the political level that it will have to be defeated. That is why I am happy to see members like the hon. member for Lapointe concern themselves with federalism.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to assure the government of my support for the Speech from the Throne. There is one part of it that I support unreservedly, namely where the government expresses its intention of granting franchise to 18-year-old Canadians. I believe all politicians in Canada, at all levels of government, are now anxious to get active participation from all classes of society. Young people have shown these last years that they could get organized so as to take part in the life of the Canadian society. Members in this house or Canadian people as a whole should not judge well-organized participation of young university students from the few acts of violence that may happen sometimes.
Of course the Speech from the Throne does not solve all the immediate problems. It does not bring any direct solution either to the problems of my constituents, but I believe a government should be strong, that it should do some planning and should not be led into quick solutions.
During this debate, the opposition and its leader seemed to talk a lot about the needs of the little man, of the poor, but they offered no solution other than to say that the government should spend more money on social welfare or other programs to solve the problem of poverty.
Mr. Speaker, I am every bit as concerned as the members of the opposition about finding a solution to the problem of poverty in Canada. There are as many poor people in my riding as anywhere else in Canada, but I believe those people trust this government; the poor as well as the others are convinced that what

October 31, 1969
The Address-Mr. Breau we need is a strong government, one that plans wisely and will, in due course, find solutions to those problems.
In his recent speech, the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau), submitted many problems to the house and drew the attention to many situations that are really disastrous. But he seems to be slightly mixed up. He said, for instance, that the fishermen should cut their own channels. Is the federal government alone to be blamed for that? It is true that it is the federal government's job to deal with the harbours and it is perhaps true that it is the federal government who is in charge of the piers. But must one blame the federal government only if some fishermen, in a given constituency, are badly organized? There are also some in mine.
But it would be unfair to blame the federal government alone. We must take constructive steps together with the provinces, and attempt to solve these problems.
The hon. member was confusing the issue, talking about social welfare, housing, all matters which come under provincial jurisdiction. But he still blamed this government for not finding an immediate solution.
The hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) has taken part in the debate and I appreciate the fact that he stressed the plight of the Newfoundland fishermen. But he did not offer any solution to the problem and was satisfied to blame the Prime Minister for being at the National Arts Center while Montreal was burning.
I wonder what relation there can be between the Prime Minister's private life and the problems which might exist in the city of Montreal? That is the type of attitude that we sometimes find in the opposition.
When the question of poverty arises in my area, it is often in reference to coastal fishermen, who are at present living under circumstances that are intolerable from many points of view.
First of all, they have no conveniences of any kind; secondly, they are not organized. When decisions are in the offing, when programs are to be announced, it is impossible for the government to find out the views of the fishermen, because they are not organized. I am happy to see that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) is in the house.
1	hope he will soon give some attention to the creation of organizations for the fishermen in order that they may find some guidance and take part in policy-making both on the federal and the provincial levels, so that such problems may be solved.
I do not think that in 1969, for example, fishermen need to get their boats on the shore without any equipment. It is true their industry is not economically sound but they should not be blamed. It is not their fault if they have been fishing in coastal waters for years. To change the situation, social development programs will be necessary. Fishermen will have to get organized and know where they stand.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?
